# Physical constraints and biological regulations underlie universal osmoresponses ## Authors - Yiyang Ye1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2411-5297](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2411-5297)) - Qirun Wang1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8845-1997](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8845-1997)) - Jie Lin1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2027-4661](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2027-4661)) † ### Affiliations 1. Center for Quantitative Biology, Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Sudies, Peking University Beijing China ([ROR:02v51f717](https://ror.org/02v51f717)) 2. Peking-Tsinghua Center for Life Sciences, Academy for Advanced Interdisciplinary Sudies, Peking University Beijing China ([ROR:02v51f717](https://ror.org/02v51f717)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Microorganisms constantly transition between environments with dramatically different external osmolarities. However, theories of microbial osmoresponse integrating physical constraints and biological regulations are lacking. Here, we propose such a theory, utilizing the separation of timescales for passive responses and active regulations. We demonstrate that regulations of osmolyte production and cell-wall synthesis assist cells in coping with intracellular crowding effects and adapting to a broad range of external osmolarity. Furthermore, we predict a threshold value above which cells cannot grow, ubiquitous across bacteria and yeast. Intriguingly, the theory predicts a dramatic speedup of cell growth after an abrupt decrease in external osmolarity due to cell-wall synthesis regulation. Our theory rationalizes the unusually fast growth observed in fission yeast after an oscillatory osmotic perturbation, and the predicted growth rate peaks match quantitatively with experimental measurements. Our study reveals the physical basis of osmoresponse, yielding far-reaching implications for microbial physiology. ## Introduction Microbes constantly transition between environments with dramatically different osmolarities, a hallmark of microbial life (Csonka, 1989; Muzzey et al., 2009; Wood, 2015; Bremer and Krämer, 2019). One of the most essential features of walled microbial cells is the turgor pressure – the elastic stress stretching the cell wall due to osmotic imbalance. Upon a hypoosmotic shock (i.e. a sudden decrease of the external osmolarity), the turgor pressure increases immediately due to the sudden water influx. To relax the turgor pressure, the cell upregulates the cell-wall synthesis rate, adds more materials to the peptidoglycan network, and eventually adapts to the lower external osmolarity (Typas et al., 2010). Upon a hyperosmotic shock (i.e. a sudden increase of the external osmolarity), the cell volume of a microbial cell shrinks within milliseconds due to water efflux, leading to a decreased turgor pressure (Rojas and Huang, 2018; Cadart et al., 2019). To increase the internal osmotic pressure, microorganisms increase their intracellular solute pool by amassing osmolyte molecules (i.e. osmoregulation), e.g., through de novo synthesis (Kempf and Bremer, 1998). The cell volume then restores progressively over time, and eventually, the cell adapts to the higher osmolarity. Intracellular crowding may act as a cell volume sensor to trigger osmoregulation (Burg, 2000; van den Berg et al., 2017; Model et al., 2021). Meanwhile, intracellular crowding due to volume reduction inevitably affects the cellular physiology globally, e.g., slowing down protein diffusion (Dix and Verkman, 2008; Dill et al., 2011; Miermont et al., 2013; Mika et al., 2014; Munder et al., 2016; Joyner et al., 2016; Molines et al., 2022) and reducing the elongation speed of translating ribosomes (Dai et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2023). Despite extensive knowledge regarding the molecular details of osmotic response pathways (Bremer and Krämer, 2019), how intracellular crowding interferes with gene expression regulation and affects osmotic adaptation remains an open question. Interestingly, many features of microbial osmoresponses appear general across different organisms, suggesting a universal underlying mechanism. For example, it is widely observed that microbial cells can adapt to a broad range of external osmolarity, with the external osmotic pressure varying over an order of magnitude (Cayley et al., 1991; Dai et al., 2018; Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017). Furthermore, the growth rate in the steady state decreases as the external osmolarity increases, and a complete arrest of cell growth occurs above a critical osmolarity (Scott, 1953; Christian and Scott, 1953; Christian, 1955; Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2018). Moreover, upon an osmotic shock, the growth rate usually does not approach the new steady-state value monotonically, e.g., an overshoot of growth rate often occurs upon a hypoosmotic shock (Rojas et al., 2017), and a damped oscillation of growth rate can happen after a hyperosmotic shock (Rojas et al., 2014). In recent experiments of Schizosaccharomyces pombe by Knapp et al., 2019, an oscillatory osmotic shock was applied to cells, during which cell volume growth was dramatically slowed down while biomass was still actively produced. Surprisingly, a supergrowth phase happened after removing the oscillatory osmotic shock, during which cells grew much faster than the steady state before the shocks. In this work, we unify all these phenomena by a theory capturing the essential elements of osmoresponses: physical constraints (e.g. the crowding effects and osmotic imbalance) and biological regulation, including osmoregulation (i.e. regulation of the osmolyte-producing protein) and cell-wall synthesis regulation. Our model assumes the following phenomenological rules: (1) the change in free water volume within the cell is driven by osmotic imbalance (Cadart et al., 2019; Rollin et al., 2023), while the remaining volume changes in proportion to protein production; (2) osmoregulation influences the production of osmolyte-producing protein, governed by intracellular protein density; (3) cell-wall synthesis is regulated through a feedback mechanism, wherein turgor pressure modulates the efficiency of cell-wall synthesis, enabling the cell to maintain a relatively stable turgor pressure; and (4) intracellular crowding slows down biochemical reactions as the protein density increases, with reactions ceasing entirely when the protein density reaches a critical threshold. Upon a hyperosmotic shock, cell volume reduction due to water efflux increases the protein density, inducing the upregulation of osmolyte-producing protein but slowing down the translation speed due to crowding. Upon a hypoosmotic shock, the dramatic water influx stretches the cell wall, and the increased turgor pressure induces cell-wall synthesis (Typas et al., 2010; Jiang and Sun, 2010; Amir and Nelson, 2012). We remark that our model is coarse-grained, without including detailed molecular mechanisms, and is therefore applicable across diverse microbial species. Notably, the predicted steady-state growth rate as a function of internal osmotic pressure from our model aligns well with experimental data from diverse organisms. This alignment allows us to quantify the sensitivities of translation speed and regulation of osmolyte-producing protein in response to intracellular density. Additionally, we demonstrate that osmoregulation and cell-wall synthesis regulation enable cells to adapt to a wide range of external osmolarities and prevent plasmolysis. Our model also predicts a non-monotonic time dependence of growth rate and protein density as they approach steady-state values following a constant osmotic shock, in concert with experimental observations (Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017). Moreover, we show that a supergrowth phase can arise following a sudden decrease in external osmolarity, driven by cell-wall synthesis regulation, either through the direct application of a hypoosmotic shock or the withdrawal of an oscillatory stimulus. Remarkably, the predicted amplitudes of supergrowth (i.e. growth rate peaks) quantitatively agree with multiple independent experimental measurements (Knapp et al., 2019). In the following Results section, we begin by outlining the primary assumptions and equations of our model in the subsection Model description, which includes four parts, each addressing one of the four phenomenological rules. Additional details can be found in Materials and methods. We then proceed to the subsection Steady states in constant environments, where we employ our theoretical framework to analyze steady-state growth and examine how the growth rate varies with external osmolarity. In the subsection Transient dynamics after a constant osmotic shock, we investigate the time-dependent osmoresponse after a constant hyperosmotic and hypoosmotic shock. Finally, in Comparison with experiments: supergrowth phenomena after osmotic oscillation, we address the supergrowth phenomena observed in S. pombe, utilizing our model to elucidate these experimental observations. ## Results ### Model description #### Cell growth In the limit of an extreme hyperosmotic shock, the remaining cytoplasmic volume is comparable to the volume of expelled water (Cayley et al., 1991; Scott Cayley et al., 2000; Miermont et al., 2013). Thus, the total cytoplasmic volume must be divided into a free volume and a bound volume (Whatmore and Reed, 1990; Cayley and Record, 2003; Lemière and Chang, 2023; Zhou et al., 2009; Rollin et al., 2023): $$ V=V_{f}+V_{b}. $$ The free volume comes from the free water that is osmotically active, and the bound volume includes the bound water $V_{bw}$ (i.e. water of macromolecular hydration) and the volume of dry mass $V_{bd}$ (Figure 1A). Because the fraction of protein mass in the total dry mass is typically constant and the volume of bound water is proportional to the dry mass (Cayley et al., 1991), the bound volume is proportional to the total protein mass $m_{p}$ through $V_{b}=\alpham_{p}$. Here, $\alpha$ is a constant, and its values for some model organisms are included in Table 1, and its detailed calculations from experimental data are in Section B of Appendix 1. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/102858/elife-102858-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) The total cytoplasmic volume includes the free and bound volumes. The free volume sets the internal osmotic pressure $Π_{in}=k_{B}TN_{a}/V_{f}$, where $V_{f}$ is the free volume and $N_{a}$ is the number of osmolyte molecules. The bound volume $V_{b}$ comprises the dry mass $V_{bd}$ and bound water $V_{bw}$, i.e., $V_{b}=V_{bd}+V_{bw}$, all proportional to the total protein mass. (B) We model osmoregulation through the change of ribosome translation strategy. When the protein density increases, the fraction of ribosomes translating the osmolyte-producing protein $χ_{a}$ is upregulated, leading to the subsequent increase in the mass fraction of the osmolyte-producing protein $ϕ_{a}$. Here, $\mu_{r}$ denotes the dry-mass growth rate. (C) The cell-wall synthesis process is controlled by the turgor pressure $\sigma$, which is proportional to the cell-wall strain $ϵ=(V−V_{cw})/V_{cw}$. The free volume changes due to osmotic imbalance, and the growth rate of the free volume follows $$ \mu_{f}≡\frac{V_{f}˙}{V_{f}}=k_{w}(Π_{in}−Π_{out}−\sigma), $$ where $Π_{in}$, $Π_{out}$ are the internal (i.e. cytoplasmic) and external osmotic pressures, respectively (Cadart et al., 2019). $Π_{in}$ is proportional to the concentration of osmolyte molecules in the free volume: $Π_{in}=k_{B}TN_{a}/V_{f}$, where $N_{a}$ is the number of osmolyte molecules, $k_{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T$ is the temperature. For simplicity, we assume that the production speed of osmolyte molecules is proportional to the mass of osmolyte-producing protein (Materials and methods). Here, we have replaced the difference of the hydrostatic pressures across the cell membrane with the turgor pressure $\sigma$, assuming that mechanical equilibrium is always satisfied. $k_{w}$ is the filtration coefficient quantifying the water permeability of the cell membrane (Solenov et al., 2017). The species of osmolytes involved in osmoregulation are diverse across different microorganisms and conditions; nevertheless, they are primarily small organic molecules (Kempf and Bremer, 1998; Empadinhas and da Costa, 2008). In this work, we simplify the problem by considering a single species of osmolyte that dominates the internal osmotic pressure, e.g., glycerol in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Reed et al., 1987; Hohmann et al., 2007; Blomberg, 2022) and glycine betaine in Escherichia coli (Wood, 2015), with the production speed proportional to the mass of the osmolyte-producing protein (Figure 1A and Materials and methods). To model gene expression regulation, we introduce $χ_{a}$ and $χ_{r}$ as the fractions of ribosomes translating the osmolyte-producing protein and ribosomal proteins (Figure 1B and Materials and methods). In steady states, $χ_{a}$ and $χ_{r}$ are equal to the mass fractions of osmolyte-producing protein and ribosomal proteins in the total proteome, $ϕ_{a}=m_{p,a}/m_{p}$ and $ϕ_{r}=m_{p,r}/m_{p}$, respectively (Scott et al., 2010; Wang and Lin, 2022). In this work, we assume that the dry-mass growth rate is proportional to the fraction of ribosomal proteins within the total proteome for simplicity, $\mu_{r}=k_{r}m_{p,r}/m_{p}=k_{r}ϕ_{r}$. This assumption leverages the fact that ribosomes are responsible for producing all proteins. The proportionality coefficient $k_{r}$ encapsulates the efficiency of ribosomal activity, being proportional to the elongation speed of the ribosome. We remark that $k_{r}$ is influenced by the crowding effect, which we address later. The growth rate of the cytoplasmic volume, $\mu=V˙/V$, is a weighted average of the free-volume growth rate $\mu_{f}$ and the dry-mass growth rate $\mu_{r}$: $$ \mu=f\mu_{f}+(1−f)\mu_{r}. $$ Here, $f$ is the free volume fraction in the total cytoplasmic volume: $f=V_{f}/V$. In this work, we refer to the growth rate as the growth rate of cytoplasmic volume μ unless otherwise mentioned. #### Osmoregulation Dai et al., 2018, found that the reduction of growth rate as the external osmolarity increases is dominated by the reduction of the translation speed $k_{r}$ instead of the ribosomal fraction $ϕ_{r}$. Therefore, we assume that the fraction of ribosomes translating themselves $χ_{r}$ is constant for simplicity. To model osmoregulation, we introduce a coupling between the fraction of ribosomes translating the osmolyte-producing protein $χ_{a}$ and the degree of intracellular crowding. We quantify the crowding effects by the protein density, defined as $ρ_{p}=m_{p}/V_{f}$, which serves as a good proxy for the dry-mass density measured in the experiments (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013; Odermatt et al., 2021) (see Table 1 and the detailed discussion on the relations between the two densities in Section A of Appendix 1) and propose the following relation: $$ χ_{a}=χ_{a}^{max}(\frac{ρ_{p}}{ρ_{c}})^{H_{a}}. $$ Here, the parameter $H_{a}$ quantifies the sensitivity of osmoregulation to intracellular crowding. $ρ_{c}$ is the critical protein density above which intracellular processes are frozen, which we introduce later in Equation 8. Therefore, $χ_{a}^{max}$ represents the largest possible $ϕ_{a}$ since all intracellular dynamics is frozen when $ρ_{p}>ρ_{c}$. We remark that our model can be directly generalized to cases where osmolyte molecules are extracted from the environment. One only needs to change the interpretation of the parameter $k_{a}$ in Equation 17 from the synthesis rate to the uptake rate, and all the results are the same. #### Cell-wall synthesis regulation In this work, the cell wall is regarded as a linear elastic material, where the turgor pressure is proportional to the elastic strain of the cell wall by a constant modulus $G$ such that $$ \sigma=Gϵ=G(\frac{V}{V_{cw}}−1). $$ Here, $V_{cw}$ is the relaxed cell-wall volume (Figure 1C). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102858.3.sa0](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102858.3.sa0)

This manuscript develops a theoretical model of osmotic pressure adaptation in microbes by osmolyte production and wall synthesis. The prediction of a rapid increase in growth rate on osmotic shock is experimentally validated using fission yeast. By using phenomenological rules rather than detailed molecular mechanisms, the model can potentially apply to a wide range of microbes, providing important insights that would be of interest to the wider community studying the regulation of cell size and mechanics. The level of coarse-graining and the assumptions and limitations of the model have been well described, providing a convincing foundation for making predictions. However, further experimental work on the validity of the core assumptions across a range of microbial organisms is needed to assess the universality of the model.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102858.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102858.3.sa1)

Summary:

A theoretical model for microbial osmoresponse was proposed. The model assumes simple phenomenological rules: (i) the change of free water volume in the cell due to osmotic imbalance based on pressure balance, (ii) osmoregulation that assumes change of the proteome partitioning depending on the osmotic pressure that affects the osmolyte-producing protein production, (iii) the cell-wall synthesis regulation where the change of the turgor pressure to cell-wall synthesis efficiency to go back to the target turgor pressure, (iv) effect of intracellular crowding assuming that the biochemical reactions slow down for more crowding and stop when the protein density (protein mass divided by free water volume) reaches a critical value. The parameter values were found in the literature or obtained by fitting to the experimental data. The authors compare the model behavior with various microorganisms (E. coli, B. subtils, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe) and successfully reproduced the overall trend (steady state behavior for many of them, dynamics for S. pombe). In addition, the model predicts non-trivial behavior such as the fast cell growth just after the hypoosmotic shock, which is consistent with experimental observation. The authors further make experimentally testable predictions regarding mutant behavior and transient dynamics.

The theory assumes simple mechanistic dependence between core variables without going into specific molecular mechanisms of regulations. The simplicity allows the theory to apply to different organisms by adjusting the time scales with parameters, and the model successfully explains broad classes of observed behaviours. Mathematically, the model provides analytical expressions of the parameter dependencies and an understanding of the dynamics through the phase space without being buried in the detail. This theory can serve as a base to discuss the universality and diversity of microbial osmoresponse.

The coarse-grained nature of the model is the strength of the model in terms of its generality. However, it does not consider various regulations at the molecular level. Hence, certain adaptation features are not considered in the current version of the model. The updated manuscript discusses the pros and cons of the current approach.

results.result: Microorganisms experience dramatic osmotic shifts in their environments, triggering immediate physical responses (water flux, turgor pressure changes) and subsequent biological adaptations (osmoregulation, cell-wall synthesis). Intracellular crowding affects cellular physiology globally, including protein diffusion and ribosomal elongation speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 establish well-documented background knowledge about microbial osmoresponse, supported by extensive citations to established literature. These claims describe known phenomena that form the foundation for the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

results.result: Microbial cells adapt to a broad range of external osmolarities (order of magnitude variation), with growth rate decreasing as osmolarity increases until complete growth arrest occurs. Growth rate approaches steady state non-monotonically after osmotic shocks, with overshoots after hypoosmotic shocks and damped oscillations after hyperosmotic shocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 describe general experimental observations across multiple species and studies, well-supported by numerous citations. These phenomena are consistently observed and form the empirical basis for model development.

results.result: In experiments by Knapp et al. (2019) on S. pombe, oscillatory osmotic shock dramatically slowed cell volume growth while biomass production continued. After removing the oscillation, cells exhibited a supergrowth phase with growth rates up to twice the reference rate, persisting for 2-3 cell cycles, with maximum growth occurring ~20 minutes after oscillation removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 and C72-C76 accurately describe experimental observations from Knapp et al. (2019). These are direct citations of published experimental results that motivated the theoretical work and provide the key phenomenon to be explained.

results.result: The model assumes four phenomenological rules: (1) free water volume changes are driven by osmotic imbalance while remaining volume changes proportionally to protein production; (2) osmoregulation is governed by intracellular protein density; (3) cell-wall synthesis is regulated by turgor pressure feedback; (4) intracellular crowding slows biochemical reactions, ceasing entirely at a critical protein density threshold.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 clearly state the model assumptions, which are reasonable simplifications supported by citations to relevant literature. The assumptions are internally consistent and form a coherent theoretical framework, though they represent coarse-grained approximations of complex biological processes.

results.result: Under extreme hyperosmotic shock, the remaining cytoplasmic volume is comparable to expelled water volume, necessitating division of total cytoplasmic volume into free volume (osmotically active water) and bound volume (bound water plus dry mass).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by multiple experimental citations and represent a fundamental structural assumption of the model that is consistent with experimental observations of extreme osmotic stress.

results.result: The model predicts a universal relationship between normalized growth rate and normalized internal osmotic pressure (Equation 10b) that fits experimental data from diverse organisms (E. coli, B. subtilis, S. cerevisiae) across different growth media.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C96 are strongly supported by Figure 2A, which shows quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data from multiple species and conditions. The universal relationship with a single parameter Hr/(Ha+1) successfully captures diverse experimental observations.

results.result: Experimental measurements show cell-wall strain remains approximately constant as external osmolarity increases, suggesting constant turgor pressure independent of external osmolarity, consistent with model assumptions.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 cite experimental measurements (Misra et al., 2013; Rojas et al., 2014) that directly support a key model prediction. The experimental validation of constant turgor pressure across osmolarity ranges strengthens the model's biological relevance.

results.result: The osmoadaptation capability of E. coli depends on growth media, presumably arising from variations in metabolic fluxes and gene expressions.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by experimental data showing different parameter values for E. coli in different media (Table 1, Figure 2A). However, the mechanistic explanation is speculative, as indicated by 'presumably.' The observation is solid but the interpretation is tentative.

results.result: Mutant cells without osmoregulation (Ha=0) cannot grow beyond mildly elevated external osmolarity, with their steady-state growth curve terminating at much lower external osmolarity than wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C46 and C97 are supported by model predictions (Figure 2B) that are consistent with previous experiments (Brewster et al., 1993). The theoretical prediction aligns with known experimental observations of osmoregulation-deficient mutants.

results.result: Mutant cells without cell-wall synthesis regulation (Hcw=0) cannot maintain constant turgor pressure as external osmolarity increases, though they grow faster than wild-type cells under the same osmolarity. These mutants are prone to plasmolysis at osmolarities where wild-type cells maintain constant turgor pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 and C98 present model predictions shown in Figure 2B-C with detailed mathematical proof in the appendix. However, these predictions have not been experimentally validated, as explicitly stated in C98. The theoretical predictions are internally consistent but require experimental confirmation.

results.result: Osmoregulation enables growth across a wide range of external osmolarities with mild protein density changes, while cell-wall synthesis regulation maintains stable turgor pressure and prevents plasmolysis. Both mechanisms expand the range of adaptable external osmolarities.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 and C24 summarize key functional insights from the model analysis, supported by the mutant simulations (Figure 2) and theoretical analysis. The conclusions logically follow from the model structure and comparative analysis of wild-type versus mutant behaviors.

results.result: Osmoresponse dynamics can be split into shock and adaptation periods. During the shock period, immediate water flow occurs with negligible mass/osmolyte production. The adaptation timescale is set by the doubling time, taking approximately one doubling time for protein density and osmolyte-producing protein fraction to reach new steady states.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C57 describe theoretical insights from the model's timescale separation, illustrated in Figure 3C-D and derived from Equations 12a-12b. The separation of timescales is a reasonable approximation supported by the model structure and consistent with experimental observations.

results.result: After a hyperosmotic shock, immediate water efflux causes instantaneous turgor pressure drop and protein density rise. Protein density initially increases (due to suppressed cell-wall volume growth from low turgor pressure) then decreases (due to osmoregulation on the doubling time scale). Growth rate approaches steady state non-monotonically via a spiral trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 and C63 describe model predictions shown in Figure 3A and 3C, with the non-monotonic behavior consistent with experimental observations from Rojas et al. (2014). The mechanistic explanations are logically derived from the model equations and timescale separation.

results.result: After a hypoosmotic shock, cells exhibit a supergrowth phase with a growth rate peak occurring ~25 minutes post-shock. This phenomenon requires a cell wall and arises from high turgor pressure driving fast cell-wall synthesis, which relaxes turgor pressure and enables faster growth. The growth rate peak increases with shock amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C71 present model predictions (Figure 3B, 3E, Appendix 1-figure 2D) with mechanistic explanations based on Equations 2, 3, and 7. The timing (~25 min) is consistent with experimental observations, and the requirement for cell walls is demonstrated by comparison with unwalled cells. The analytical expression (Equation 13) provides theoretical support.

results.result: The model successfully recapitulates the supergrowth phase and gradually increasing protein/dry-mass density during osmotic oscillation perturbation. Predicted growth rate peaks versus period length and number of periods quantitatively match experimental data from Knapp et al. (2019) without additional fitting.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C82, and C100 describe quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data shown in Figure 4. The model was fit only to the amplitude dependence (Figure 4D) to obtain Hcw and τcw+, then predictions for period length (Figure 4B) and number of periods (Figure 4C) matched data without further fitting, providing strong validation.

results.result: Cell-wall synthesis regulation is crucial for the supergrowth phenomenon, as unwalled cells do not exhibit supergrowth after periodic perturbation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78 and C101 are supported by model predictions shown in Appendix 1-figure 3 and detailed analysis in Section E of Appendix 1. The comparison between walled and unwalled cells clearly demonstrates the necessity of cell-wall synthesis regulation for supergrowth.

results.result: An infinitely long periodic osmotic shock can be equivalently mapped to a constant osmotic shock, having the same time-averaged growth rate and protein density in steady states.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 present a theoretical result with detailed proof in Section D of Appendix 1 and illustration in Appendix 1-figure 2F. This is a mathematical consequence of the model structure and provides useful theoretical insight.

results.result: Switching from a long hyperosmotic period to reference medium is equivalent to a hypoosmotic shock, with growth rate peak increasing with amplitude. Beyond a critical amplitude, cytoplasm becomes completely jammed during hyperosmotic shock, eliminating the supergrowth phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 provide mechanistic explanation for the non-monotonic relationship between growth rate peak and oscillation amplitude (Figure 4D-E). The explanation is logically derived from the model's crowding effects and is consistent with the kink point observed in simulations.

results.result: The theory captures steady-state properties of constant turgor pressure and reduced growth rate with increasing external osmolarity. Growth rate reduction is due to free water loss and subsequent intracellular crowding. The model predicts a critical external osmolarity above which cell growth is completely inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 summarize key theoretical predictions validated by experimental data (Figure 2A). The mechanistic explanation for growth rate reduction is logically derived from the model structure, and the critical osmolarity prediction is consistent with experimental observations across species.

results.result: The model predicts non-monotonic time dependence of protein density after a constant hyperosmotic shock.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 3A and explained mechanistically by claims C59-C61. This prediction is a direct consequence of the model dynamics and timescale separation.

results.result: Knapp et al. (2019) observed rapid repolarization of cell-wall glucan synthase Bgs4 to the cell tip following removal of osmotic oscillations in fission yeast, in agreement with the dynamics of cell-wall synthesis efficiency predicted from the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 compare experimental observations (Knapp et al., 2019, Figure S4H) with model predictions (Figure 4-figure supplement 1), showing qualitative agreement. This provides independent validation of the model's cell-wall synthesis regulation dynamics.

results.result: Model predictions are consistent with the growth rate peak after a hypoosmotic shock observed for B. subtilis.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 cites consistency with experimental observations from Rojas et al. (2017). This extends the model's applicability beyond S. pombe to another organism, though quantitative comparison is not shown.

results.result: The model is a coarse-grained framework that neglects molecular details of gene expression regulation, does not account for interaction between cell growth and osmolyte production, assumes constant ribosomal protein fraction, and does not include osmolyte export, membrane tension effects on peptidoglycan precursor flux, or memory effects in regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C108, C114-C115, and C118-C119 explicitly acknowledge model limitations. These are honest assessments of what the model does not include, appropriately documented for transparency. The limitations are reasonable for a coarse-grained theoretical framework.

results.result: Shen et al. (2023) found that cells exhibited stronger osmotic gene expression response under glucose-limited conditions than glucose-rich conditions, because glycolysis intermediates were limited, requiring more glycerol-production enzyme expression for stress adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 accurately summarize findings from Shen et al. (2023). This is cited as related work that addresses molecular mechanisms not included in the current coarse-grained model.

results.result: Microorganisms can exhibit memory effects to external stimuli. In yeast osmoregulation, short-term memory (facilitated by posttranslational regulation of trehalose metabolism) and long-term memory (orchestrated by transcription factors and mRNP granules) have been identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 cite established literature on microbial memory effects (Mitchell et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2020). This is discussed as a phenomenon not captured by the current model, which assumes instantaneous regulation.

results.result: By leveraging timescale separation, the model facilitates in-depth analytical and numerical analysis of process interactions during cellular adaptation, offering a valuable tool for understanding microbial osmoresponse phenomena and developing predictive models for microbial behaviors under osmotic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 summarize the contribution and significance of the theoretical framework. The claims are supported by the demonstrated analytical insights (e.g., Equations 10a-10b, 12a-12b) and quantitative predictions matching experimental data.

results.result: Experiments suggest turgor pressure induces cell-wall synthesis through multiple mechanisms: mechanosensors on cell membrane (S. pombe), increasing peptidoglycan network pore size, and accelerating cell-wall synthesis machinery movement (E. coli).
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 cite experimental literature (Dupres et al., 2009; Neeli-Venkata et al., 2021; Typas et al., 2010; Amir and Nelson, 2012) supporting the biological basis for the model's cell-wall synthesis regulation mechanism.

results.result: In plasmolysis, insertion of newly synthesized cell-wall materials is interrupted immediately due to membrane-wall separation. Upregulation of cell-wall synthesis rate takes longer, involving processes like polarisome complex reorientation, actin polarization, and machinery delivery in fungi.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 provide biological justification for the asymmetric timescales (τcw+ >> τcw-) in Equation 7. The reasoning is supported by citations to relevant literature on fungal cell-wall synthesis (Kono et al., 2012; Haupt et al., 2018).

results.result: Experiments show cytoplasm of bacteria, yeast, and mammalian cells resembles crowded colloidal suspensions with significantly reduced biomolecule mobility (a signature of glass transition), affecting biochemical processes globally. The model assumes osmolyte production, translational elongation, and cell-wall synthesis are all slowed by the same crowding factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C151 cite extensive experimental literature on cytoplasmic crowding effects and justify the model's crowding factor (Equation 8). The assumption that all processes are affected by the same crowding factor is a simplification, but reasonable for a coarse-grained model.

results.result: At steady state, proportions of all components (free water volume, cell mass, cell-wall volume) must be constant relative to total cell volume to ensure homeostasis, requiring all growth rates to be equal.
results.evaluation: Claim C156 states a fundamental principle of steady-state growth that is mathematically necessary for homeostasis. This is a well-established concept in cell biology and forms the basis for steady-state analysis.

results.result: Abrupt water flux occurs within hundreds of milliseconds after an osmotic shock, allowing estimation of water permeability kw ~ 100 min⁻¹ atm⁻¹.
results.evaluation: Claim C159 cites experimental observations (Boer et al., 2011) used to estimate a model parameter and justify neglecting the μf/kw term in Equation 9. The timescale estimate is reasonable and consistent with the model's timescale separation.

results.result: Upon hyperosmotic shock, cell volume reduction increases protein density, inducing osmolyte-producing protein upregulation but slowing translation due to crowding. Upon hypoosmotic shock, water influx stretches the cell wall, and increased turgor pressure induces cell-wall synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 describe immediate consequences of osmotic shocks as inferred from the model assumptions and known biological responses. These are logical predictions from the model structure supported by citations.

results.result: The model predicts non-monotonic time dependence of growth rate and protein density approaching steady-state values following a constant osmotic shock, consistent with experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 summarizes a key dynamic prediction (shown in Figure 3A) that is consistent with cited experimental observations (Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017). This demonstrates the model captures transient dynamics, not just steady states.

results.result: A supergrowth phase can arise following a sudden decrease in external osmolarity, driven by cell-wall synthesis regulation, either through direct hypoosmotic shock or withdrawal of oscillatory stimulus.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 presents a major theoretical prediction that is subsequently validated by quantitative comparison with experimental data (Figure 4). This is a central result of the paper.

results.result: Predicted amplitudes of supergrowth (growth rate peaks) quantitatively agree with multiple independent experimental measurements from Knapp et al. (2019).
results.evaluation: Claim C27 is strongly supported by Figure 4B-D, showing quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data across different oscillation parameters. This is the strongest validation of the model.

results.result: Reduced turgor pressure is detrimental to multiple biological processes, e.g., cytokinesis in fission yeast requires turgor pressure participation.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 cites experimental evidence (Proctor et al., 2012) for the biological importance of maintaining turgor pressure, supporting the functional significance of cell-wall synthesis regulation.

results.result: The assumption that dry-mass growth rate is proportional to ribosomal protein fraction leverages the fact that ribosomes are responsible for producing all proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 provides biological justification for a key model assumption (μr = krϕr). This is a reasonable simplification based on fundamental cell biology.

results.result: The model is built on four phenomenological rules: (1) free water volume changes driven by osmotic imbalance while remaining volume changes proportionally to protein production, (2) osmoregulation governed by intracellular protein density, (3) cell-wall synthesis regulated by turgor pressure feedback, and (4) intracellular crowding slowing biochemical reactions with complete cessation at a critical protein density threshold. The model also divides cytoplasmic volume into free and bound components.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept the model's phenomenological framework. Reviewer 1 states the model 'assumes simple phenomenological rules' and lists all four core assumptions without critique. Reviewer 2 notes 'the level of coarse-graining and the assumptions and limitations of the model have been well described, providing a convincing foundation for making predictions.' No reviewer challenges these foundational assumptions.

results.result: The model predicts steady-state properties including constant turgor pressure and reduced growth rate with increasing external osmolarity, with growth rate reduction attributed to free water loss and intracellular crowding. The model predicts a critical external osmolarity above which growth is completely inhibited and establishes a universal relationship between normalized growth rate and normalized internal osmotic pressure that fits data from bacteria and yeast.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the model 'successfully reproduced the overall trend (steady state behavior for many of them)' across multiple organisms. Reviewer 2 notes the model provides 'important insights' and that predictions align 'well with experimental data from diverse organisms.' The universal relationship fitting multiple species data is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The model demonstrates that osmoregulation and cell-wall synthesis regulation enable adaptation to wide osmolarity ranges and prevent plasmolysis. Mutant cells without osmoregulation cannot grow even at mildly elevated osmolarity, while mutants without cell-wall synthesis regulation grow faster than wild-type but cannot maintain turgor pressure and are prone to plasmolysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the model 'make experimentally testable predictions regarding mutant behavior' without expressing doubt. Reviewer 2 states the model has 'well described' assumptions providing 'a convincing foundation for making predictions.' The mutant predictions (C46 consistent with Brewster et al., 1993; C98 proposed for experimental validation) are treated as logical extensions of the model framework.

results.result: The model predicts non-monotonic dynamics following osmotic shocks, with osmoresponse split into shock and adaptation periods. After hyperosmotic shock, protein density initially increases then decreases, with the timescale set by doubling time. Growth rate approaches steady state non-monotonically via spiral trajectories in phase space.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the model 'successfully reproduced the overall trend...dynamics for S. pombe' and notes consistency with experimental observations (C63 references Rojas et al., 2014). The phase space analysis and timescale separation are accepted as part of the model's analytical strength, with Reviewer 1 noting the model 'provides analytical expressions of the parameter dependencies and an understanding of the dynamics through the phase space.'

results.result: The model predicts a supergrowth phase following hypoosmotic shock, with growth rate peaks occurring ~25 minutes post-shock. This phenomenon is driven by cell-wall synthesis regulation: high turgor pressure induces rapid cell-wall synthesis, which relaxes pressure and enables faster growth. Unwalled cells do not exhibit supergrowth, confirming cell-wall synthesis regulation is crucial. Growth rate peaks increase with shock amplitude.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly validates this finding: 'The prediction of a rapid increase in growth rate on osmotic shock is experimentally validated using fission yeast.' Reviewer 1 states the model 'predicts non-trivial behavior such as the fast cell growth just after the hypoosmotic shock, which is consistent with experimental observation.' The mechanistic explanation and role of cell-wall regulation are accepted without challenge.

results.result: The model successfully recapitulates experimental observations from Knapp et al. 2019 on oscillatory osmotic shocks in S. pombe, including supergrowth phase, increasing protein/dry-mass density during perturbation, and growth rate peaks ~20 min after oscillation removal. Predicted growth rate peaks versus period length and number of periods quantitatively match experimental data without additional fitting. The model also predicts equivalence between infinitely long periodic shocks and constant shocks, and explains the non-monotonic amplitude dependence with a critical jamming threshold.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 emphasizes this as strong validation: the model 'successfully reproduced the overall trend...dynamics for S. pombe' and notes 'As a strong support of our theory, the predicted growth rate peaks quantitatively agree with the experimental data without additional fitting.' Reviewer 2 states 'They validate their model predictions...experimentally using fission yeast.' The quantitative agreement without further fitting (C82, C100) is highlighted as particularly convincing evidence.

results.result: The model is acknowledged as coarse-grained, neglecting molecular details of gene expression regulation, osmolyte export, interaction between biomass and osmolyte production, memory effects, and membrane tension effects. The framework assumes instantaneous cellular state-dependent regulation rather than incorporating temporal memory.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly addresses this: 'The coarse-grained nature of the model is the strength of the model in terms of its generality. However, it does not consider various regulations at the molecular level. Hence, certain adaptation features are not considered in the current version of the model. The updated manuscript discusses the pros and cons of the current approach.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the level of coarse-graining and the assumptions and limitations of the model have been well described.' Both reviewers accept these limitations as reasonable trade-offs for generality.

results.result: By leveraging timescale separation, the model facilitates analytical and numerical analysis of process interactions during cellular adaptation, offering a valuable tool for understanding microbial osmoresponse and developing predictive models for behaviors under osmotic stress.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Mathematically, the model provides analytical expressions of the parameter dependencies and an understanding of the dynamics through the phase space without being buried in the detail. This theory can serve as a base to discuss the universality and diversity of microbial osmoresponse.' Reviewer 2 notes the model 'can potentially apply to a wide range of microbes, providing important insights that would be of interest to the wider community studying the regulation of cell size and mechanics.'

results.result: Background claims establish that microorganisms transition between environments with different osmolarities, respond via turgor pressure changes and osmoregulation, experience intracellular crowding effects on physiology, can adapt to broad osmolarity ranges with decreasing growth rates, and exhibit non-monotonic growth dynamics including supergrowth phases as observed in S. pombe experiments by Knapp et al. 2019.
results.evaluation: These are background/contextual claims establishing the biological phenomena the model addresses. No reviewer challenges these established observations, which are well-supported by the extensive citations provided. Reviewers focus their evaluation on the model's ability to explain these phenomena rather than questioning the phenomena themselves.

results.result: Experimental measurements show cell-wall strain remains approximately constant as external osmolarity increases, suggesting constant turgor pressure independent of external osmolarity. Osmoadaptation capability depends on growth media, presumably due to variations in metabolic fluxes and gene expression.
results.evaluation: These experimental observations from literature (C37-38 from Misra et al. 2013, Rojas et al. 2014; C44 from multiple sources) are cited to support model assumptions. Reviewers do not challenge these literature-based claims. Reviewer 2 notes the model assumptions are 'well described, providing a convincing foundation,' implicitly accepting the experimental basis.

results.result: Model predictions are consistent with growth rate peaks after hypoosmotic shock observed in B. subtilis.
results.evaluation: This cross-species validation is mentioned as consistent with Rojas et al. 2017 data. While not extensively discussed by reviewers, it falls under Reviewer 1's statement that the model 'successfully reproduced the overall trend' across 'various microorganisms (E. coli, B. subtils, S. cerevisiae, S. pombe).' The consistency with B. subtilis data supports the model's generality.

results.result: Supporting mechanistic details include experimental evidence for turgor pressure inducing cell-wall synthesis through multiple mechanisms, cytoplasm resembling crowded colloidal suspensions with reduced biomolecule mobility, crowding effects on biochemical processes, steady-state homeostasis requirements, and rapid water flux timescales after osmotic shock.
results.evaluation: These are detailed mechanistic claims supporting the model framework, all backed by literature citations. Reviewers accept the model's mechanistic basis without challenging these specific details. Reviewer 2's statement that assumptions are 'well described, providing a convincing foundation' encompasses acceptance of this mechanistic grounding.
